question.note: Whether the substance use-friendship link from heterogeneous schools holds in AI-majority schools: Q2, and the substance-use question Q3.

flags.text: The note says prevention programs 'may be ineffective in AI contexts'; the paper says common network intervention strategies 'may not be as effective as previously thought' (p.16).

question.note: Not a question. The presumption of network-based prevention that ties are founded on substance use, disputed by the findings, is I6 (as the earlier judge credited a similar entry).

Reciprocity, transitivity and degree effects (preferential attachment or egalitarian constraints, p.4) asked about: Q4. The p.14 quote is reported as part of the question, not as a finding. 'Compared to other settings' follows the paper's indirect comparison; not Q-x2 (no tested comparison claimed).

central_claim.note: C1 in full ('rather than risky behaviors' is the abstract's wording). 'Unlike in other populations' gives the contrast of C2 without naming heterogeneous settings or 'weaker organizing principle'; partial. Exceptions not named, no catch.

evidence.note: Network data from 9th/10th graders in three Northern Plains reservation schools (E1, as the earlier judge credited without 'cross-sectional'). 247 is the abstract's analysis N and is not paired with 77% or the per-school survey counts in the claim (the p.6 quote gives those, correctly, for 263): E2 partial. ERGMs named only: E3 partial.
Structural terms and actor attributes of the models (E3 part); measures not specified, so no E5.
Network Canvas, directed nominations, up to 10 closest friends.
Peer-perception imputation with the paper's rule (more than half of incoming nominators, response >= 2); sensitivity analysis not mentioned.
CES-D, six questions (p.7); depression part of E5.
Six-item MEIM adaptation; AI identity part of E5. Binary substance use measures never stated in this note, so E5 is not joined.
AMEs via ergMargins, comparable across the three school networks.
Diagnostics are accurate (p.12) but not in the gold. Strictly, trace plots assessed chain mixing and the MCMLE criterion assessed convergence; too small to flag.
ERGMs by MCMC MLE in R; the quote says 'within each school'.
AMEs for the non-linear scaling of ERGM coefficients; repeats E3.
Convergence criterion, 12 models within 25 iterations, no degeneracy: accurate (p.12), not in the gold.
Goodness of fit, accurate (p.12), not in the gold.
Structural terms (reciprocity, GWESP, degree); repeats E3.

key_findings.note: 'Primary drivers' is the abstract's wording (F-n1 characterization); reciprocity and transitivity named, all three schools.

Abstract's wording: no consistent sending/receiving association. Homophily and the two exceptions not stated, so partial. 'Diverging from prior research in non-AI populations' is the paper's own contrast (p.1, p.13).

flags.text: The note says homophily on gender, grade and sexual orientation was significant and consistent across the schools; the paper says this of gender and grade only ('across all schools'), and says sexual orientation homophily was 'also significant and positive'. Table 3 shows it non-significant for the non-straight category in School B and only marginal (p<0.10) for straight students in School C.

key_findings.note: Gender, grade and sexual orientation homophily: F3 in full; the cross-school consistency is stretched for sexual orientation.

flags.text: The note says Schools A and B 'showed egalitarian constraints on popularity'; the paper reports only that their indegree distributions did not deviate from chance and says this 'may reflect the stronger operation of egalitarian norms' (p.14, p.15). The cultural interpretation is stated as a finding.

key_findings.note: Incoming ties centralized only in School C is one half of F5 (outdegree centralization in all schools not stated); the School C alcohol sender effect is a detail of F1.
Structural-terms-plus-substance-use models give the same nulls (p.14).
Where the homophily exceptions occurred (School B; the quote gives alcohol p<0.01 and marijuana p<0.10 with its qualifier): a detail of F1. 'Suggesting size-dependent' is hedged and close to p.15-16.

flags.text: The note says AI identity homophily was non-significant 'because' racial identity is near-universal; the paper says the null 'is consistent with several contextual considerations' and gives this as the first of three (p.15).

key_findings.note: AI identity homophily null is the AI identity half of F4; the earlier judge flagged the same 'because'.

flags.text: The note says the density range reflects 'differences in institutional environments'; the quoted sentence says it reflects 'the low-to-moderate tie density typical of friendship nomination networks', and only School C's higher density is said to 'may reflect' its residential setting (p.13).

key_findings.note: The density figures are accurate and not in the gold; the explanation is the note's.

scope_and_limits.note: Three schools on one reservation, may not extend to heterogeneous schools (L1); 'other developmental epochs' mentions developmental stage (L4, per the decided note). Grounded through the in-paper p.16 developmental-epoch quote.
Cross-sectional with both consequences (selection vs influence, association vs cause).
Peer perceptions can be biased (false consensus, network norms); the consequence that imputation could inflate similarity among friends is not stated.
Local governance of sovereign reservations: accurate to p.17 (offered there as future research), not in the gold; as the earlier judge decided.
Association versus cause without naming the design; repeats the id.

theoretical_positioning.note: Moving beyond generalizations from heterogeneous settings is the testing half of T3 (paper's wording), without what is replicated and what is disputed; as the earlier judge credited.
Challenging the assumptions underpinning network-based prevention programs is C3 ('challenge' is the paper's word), a central claim; credited as misplaced, as the earlier judge did.

flags.text: The note says the authors argue that 'conventional models do not hold' in their context; the paper says 'the conventional assumption ... that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study' (p.16) and keeps the standard network framework.

theoretical_positioning.note: Departure from established trends is the disputing half of T3; repeats the id.

interlocutor_claim.note: The conventional 'risky behavior is a primary determinant' assumption, disputed (I4; p.16 'does not hold in our study'). Mentions network intervention strategies, part of I6, without the presumption that ties are founded on substance use being spelled out.

flags.text: The note says the paper disputes the Rees, Freng and Winfree finding that AI adolescents in heterogeneous schools had fewer reciprocated friendships; the paper cites that finding without contesting it, builds on the study and notes only that it was descriptive (p.2), and the limitations say those heterogeneous schools showed 'different network characteristics' (p.16).

interlocutor_claim.note: Substance correct (finding, descriptive analysis), stance wrong: half credit and a flag.
Builds on Schaefer, Kornienko and Fox; framing of sender (withdrawal) effects follows p.4.
